source_refs.note: Topic 22.3, printed pages 88-89 (PDF 91-92): the six methods (i-vi) as printed, each followed by the book's reaction scheme as a diagram.

blocks.text: Alcohols can be prepared from alkenes, halogenoalkanes, carbonyl compounds, carboxylic acids, and esters.
i) When hot steam is reacted with an alkene, using concentrated phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) as a catalyst, electrophilic addition takes place to form an alcohol.

blocks.alt: Displayed ethene + H2O(g), with H3PO4 over the arrow and heat under it, gives displayed ethanol. Labels: ethene, steam, ethanol.
blocks.caption: i) Ethene and steam to ethanol (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 91).

blocks.text: ii. Alcohols are obtained by the oxidation of alkenes with cold, dilute KMnO₄, a mild oxidising agent.

blocks.alt: Displayed ethene + H2O + [O], with KMnO4 over the arrow and OH- under it, gives displayed ethane-1,2-diol, HO-CH2-CH2-OH. Labels: ethene, ethane-1,2-diol.
blocks.caption: ii) Oxidation of alkenes using cold, dilute KMnO4 to form a diol (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 91).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed caption reads 'to from a diol'; it should read 'to form a diol'.
iii) The halogen atom in halogenoalkanes can be substituted by –OH group when heated with aqueous NaOH in a nucleophilic substitution reaction, giving an alcohol.

blocks.alt: Displayed bromoethane + NaOH, with Heat over the arrow, gives displayed ethanol + NaBr. Labels: bromoethane, ethanol.
blocks.caption: iii) Bromoethane and aqueous sodium hydroxide to ethanol (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 92).

blocks.text: iv) Aldehydes and ketones can be reduced by reducing agents such as NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄ to obtain alcohols. Aldehydes are reduced to primary alcohols. Ketones are reduced to secondary alcohols.

blocks.alt: Two equations with LiAlH4 over the arrow. Displayed ethanal (C=O with H) + 2[H] gives displayed ethanol, labelled primary alcohol. Displayed propanone (C=O in the middle of three carbons) + 2[H] gives propan-2-ol, OH on the middle carbon, labelled secondary alcohol.
blocks.caption: iv) Reduction of ethanal and propanone (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 92).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed label 'secondary alchol' is misspelt; it is secondary alcohol.
v) Similarly, carboxylic acids are reduced by LiAlH₄ to primary alcohols.

blocks.alt: Displayed ethanoic acid (C=O with OH) + 4[H], with LiAlH4 over the arrow, gives displayed ethanol + H2O. Labels: ethanoic acid, ethanol.
blocks.caption: v) Reduction of ethanoic acid to ethanol (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 92).

blocks.text: vi) When an ester is heated with dilute acid or alkali, hydrolysis takes place and a carboxylic acid and alcohol are formed.

blocks.alt: CH3-C(=O)-O-CH2-CH3 + H2O, with H+(aq) over equilibrium arrows, gives CH3-C(=O)-OH + CH3-CH2-OH. Labels: ethyl ethanoate, ethanoic acid.
blocks.caption: vi) Hydrolysis of ethyl ethanoate (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 92).
